## Linear Gaussian Bayesian networks

In a linear Gaussian network each variable is a linear function of its
parents plus independent normal noise:
$$X_i = \beta_{i0} + \sum_{j \in \mathrm{Pa}(i)} \beta_{ij} X_j + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma_i^2).$$
The joint distribution is multivariate normal, and every conditional is
available in closed form.

```{r}
g <- bayesian_network(list(c("Rainfall", "Yield"), c("Fertilizer", "Yield"), c("Yield", "Price")))
g <- add_cpd(g, lg_cpd("Rainfall", intercept = 600, sd = 100))
g <- add_cpd(g, lg_cpd("Fertilizer", intercept = 50, sd = 10))
g <- add_cpd(g, lg_cpd("Yield", intercept = 1, coefficients = c(Rainfall = 0.004, Fertilizer = 0.03), sd = 0.5))
g <- add_cpd(g, lg_cpd("Price", intercept = 300, coefficients = c(Yield = -20), sd = 15))
check_model(g)
joint <- gaussian_joint(g)
gaussian_moments(joint)
```

Queries condition the joint Gaussian. A low price is evidence of a large
harvest, and therefore of more rain:

```{r}
q <- query(g, "Rainfall", list(Price = 150))
gaussian_moments(q)
```

Interventions cut incoming arcs. Setting the price by decree tells us
nothing about rain:

```{r}
gaussian_moments(gaussian_query(g, "Rainfall", interventions = list(Price = 150)))
gaussian_moments(gaussian_query(g, "Price", interventions = list(Fertilizer = 70)))
```

## Gaussian factors

Internally, computations use canonical form $\exp(-\tfrac12 x^\top K x + h^\top x + g)$,
in which products are sums and conditioning is a slice:

```{r}
f <- gaussian_factor(c("X", "Y"), mean = c(0, 1), covariance = matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 2), 2))
gaussian_moments(gaussian_reduce(f, c(Y = 3)))
gaussian_moments(gaussian_marginalize(f, "Y"))
```

## Learning

Maximum likelihood for a linear Gaussian CPD is least squares regression on
the parents:

```{r}
d <- simulate_bn(g, 2000, seed = 1)
fit <- fit_parameters(bayesian_network(edges(g)), d)
get_cpd(fit, "Yield")
```

## Conditional Gaussian (hybrid) networks

A conditional Gaussian network allows discrete parents of continuous
variables (never continuous parents of discrete ones). Each configuration of
the discrete parents selects its own regression.

```{r}
hb <- bayesian_network(list(c("Species", "Length"), c("Species", "Weight"), c("Length", "Weight")))
hb <- add_cpd(hb, cpd("Species", c(trout = 0.7, salmon = 0.3)))
hb <- add_cpd(hb, cg_cpd("Length", "Species", list(Species = c("trout", "salmon")),
                         intercept = c(40, 65), sd = c(5, 8)))
hb <- add_cpd(hb, cg_cpd("Weight", "Species", list(Species = c("trout", "salmon")),
                         intercept = c(-1, -2),
                         coefficients = matrix(c(0.05, 0.08), 2, dimnames = list(NULL, "Length")),
                         sd = c(0.3, 0.5), continuous_parents = "Length"))
is_hybrid_bn(hb)
post <- query(hb, c("Species", "Length"), list(Weight = 2))
post
```

The posterior of the continuous variables is a mixture of normals, one
component per discrete configuration; inference enumerates the discrete
configurations exactly, so it is limited to models with a moderate number
of them (`max_configurations`).

## Gaussian Markov networks and Gaussian belief propagation

An undirected Gaussian model is specified by its precision matrix. Gaussian
belief propagation computes the exact means on any graph where it
converges, and the exact variances on trees.

```{r}
K <- matrix(c(4, -1, 0, -1, 4, -1, 0, -1, 4), 3, dimnames = rep(list(c("A", "B", "C")), 2))
gm <- gaussian_markov_network(K, h = c(1, 0, 2))
gbp <- gaussian_bp(gm)
gbp$mean
solve(K, c(1, 0, 2))
```
